title: SpaceX Misses Booster Recovery in Gulf Explosion, but Starship Spacecraft Reaches Orbit
snippet: SpaceX's bold attempt at a historic 'double catch' was cut short Friday when its Super Heavy booster was diverted into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded. However, the Starship upper stage successfully reached orbit to continue its high-stakes test mission.
content:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas — SpaceX’s ambitious effort to pull off an unprecedented "double catch" fell short on Friday after its giant rocket booster was diverted into the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded on impact. Despite the setback, the mission remains a major step forward as the Starship upper stage successfully reached orbit for its boldest test flight yet.

The 407-foot rocket system lifted off from SpaceX’s Starbase facility in South Texas, but safety protocols triggered a diversion for the 236-foot Super Heavy booster away from the launch pad. The loss meant Elon Musk's space launch company missed out on retrieving both main components of the vehicle simultaneously.

“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice said during the broadcast, emphasizing that safety checks take priority to protect pad infrastructure. Company officials did not immediately provide a technical explanation for the diversion.

A High-Stakes Orbital Demonstration

Despite the booster's plunge into the sea, the 171-foot Starship spacecraft surged into space, successfully deploying 26 advanced Starlink satellites shortly after reaching orbit. The spacecraft is scheduled to complete 15 laps around Earth at an altitude of roughly 170 miles before attempting a dramatic return to the launch pad on Saturday.

If successful, mechanical arms attached to the launch tower—commonly referred to as "chopsticks"—will attempt to grab the returning spacecraft out of midair. While SpaceX has previously landed boosters using tower arms three times, catching the upper-stage spacecraft from orbit represents a historic first.

Paving the Path to the Moon and Mars

The upgraded Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, designed to be fully reusable to drastically reduce the cost of space travel. Musk envisions a fleet of Starships eventually replacing SpaceX's workhorse Falcon rockets to enable continuous launch schedules for lunar bases and Mars missions.

“That’s how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” SpaceX Vice President of Launch Kiko Dontchev said at a recent NASA summit, highlighting the company's long-term goal of total vehicle reusability.

The test flight holds enormous weight for NASA, which has awarded SpaceX billions of dollars to use Starship as the human landing system for its Artemis lunar program. NASA expects to return astronauts to the moon as early as 2028, with NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman praising the mission's progress on social media following Starship's successful orbital insertion.
